messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Architect
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Aman was a 41-year-old South Asian man who had come to treatment after nearly a year of trying to carry on as if nothing had changed. He lived with his wife, worked as an architect, and on the surface still functioned well enough to keep up appearances, but in private he described a life that had narrowed around a single period of violence with a former romantic partner. The relationship had once seemed promising and, in his telling, had been marked by trust he thought was safe. That trust collapsed when his partner began physically assaulting him in episodes that left him afraid not only of the blows themselves but of what might happen if he resisted, spoke up, or tried to leave. He did not describe the details as a continuous story at first; instead he seemed to present the experience in fragments, as though the events were still too close to view all at once. What he returned to most often was the sense of being trapped with someone he had trusted, and the shameful certainty that he had failed in the role he believed he should have held in life, both as a partner and as a man who should have known how to protect himself.

After the assaults ended, Aman began noticing that ordinary bodily sensations could jolt him back into the same state of fear. When he felt physically unwell, even in minor ways, he became unsettled and preoccupied, as if the weakness in his body meant danger was already near. He described moments at work when he would suddenly feel faint, feverish, or simply “off,” and then find himself scanning for signs that something bad was about to happen. Similar spikes in unease came when he heard incomprehensible chatter, especially in crowded public places or office settings where different conversations blurred together. In those moments, the sound of voices he could not make out seemed to him like the confusion and loss of control of those earlier episodes, and he would tense before he could fully understand why. He was also intensely affected by the smell of alcohol. If he passed someone who had been drinking, or entered a social setting where alcohol was present, his stomach tightened and his attention fixed on escape routes, because the odor had become tied in his mind to danger and humiliation.

Aman described himself as living in a constant state of alertness. He said his body reacted to danger before he had even had time to think, with a sudden surge of tension and a startled jolt that left him embarrassed in public. He became easily jumpy at small noises, especially when he was alone in his office late in the day or when someone came up behind him unexpectedly at the drafting table. Sleep also became difficult. He would lie in bed feeling that he needed to stay alert, monitoring the apartment long after his wife had fallen asleep, unwilling to let himself drift fully off. On some nights he would check his phone repeatedly or remain half-upright for hours, telling himself that if he relaxed too much he might miss something important. He recognized that this was wearing him down, but he also felt that remaining watchful was the only thing that made sense to him.

When the assaults came back to him, they did so with a force that felt immediate rather than remembered. Aman said that remembering the event brought back the same terror he had felt at the time, and he described the memories not as a smooth narrative but as a series of brief, frozen moments. Each moment appeared in his mind like a picture, separated from the next, and he often felt as though he were looking at photographs rather than recalling an event in the usual way. He could not move through the memory steadily; instead, he was hit by isolated images, each carrying the same intensity as if it were happening again. The most distressing part for him was not simply that he could recall what happened, but that the feeling in his body returned with the images, leaving him shaken long after the memory had passed.

Over time, Aman began organizing his days around avoiding anything that might trigger those reactions. He became careful about where he sat in restaurants, avoided social events where alcohol might be served, and found himself increasingly reluctant to spend long stretches in busy environments where background chatter merged into something he could not parse. As an architect, he had to move between site visits, client meetings, and office work, and these settings now felt complicated in ways they had not before. On days when he was physically unwell or exhausted, he noticed his vigilance intensify, making it harder to concentrate during design reviews or to tolerate the noise of colleagues speaking at once. He had continued showing up, but with more effort, more concealment, and more strain.

By the time he sought help, Aman was no longer able to dismiss the extent of what he was experiencing. He had started to see how much of his life was being shaped by the need to stay on guard and by the conviction that he could not trust himself to do the right thing if another crisis came. He felt betrayed by someone he had trusted, ashamed that he had not been able to prevent what happened, and frightened by how easily his body still responded as if the danger were present. What brought him in finally was the realization that he could not keep living this way with his wife and at work, always braced, always scanning, and he hoped treatment might help him feel safe enough to sleep, to be around people again, and to believe that his life was no longer defined by what had been done to him.
